\paragraph{Drafter's summary.} logit P(churn) = -1.96 + a small linear backbone over 27 inputs (all $|$w$|$ $<$= 0.32 per SD; state offsets up to -1.9 logit) + an international-plan switch (+2.91 logit) + an always-on voicemail-plan/\allowbreak{}state:41 offset unit (-0.54, -1.04) + exact single-state offsets + usage\_\allowbreak{}response, all additive in the logit. All nonlinearity is in usage\_\allowbreak{}response: a usage hinge (day/evening/night minutes, never active for voicemail-plan customers, on from about 190 day minutes), a steeper second hinge for heavy users (from about 240 day minutes), and a service-calls gate (shut for 0-2 calls, opening from 3) that is closed again by usage, so service calls matter only for light users. Train AUC 0.919, accuracy 0.921. This retrained elite copy of the 10-seed churn100-s7 genome (same key 20708, generation 98) has the same three-part usage response and intl-plan switch; the weights differ slightly (e.g. intl plan +2.91 here vs +2.88).

\paragraph{What resisted explanation.} Nothing structural (5 input splits, no hidden splits, no consolidation). The service-calls gate (4344) and the heavy-use hinge (14351 -$>$ 10552) take the usage hinge 879 as their only hidden input, so they sit as own nodes of the usage\_\allowbreak{}response composition rather than in leaves (a leaf cannot take another annotation's exit as an entry). Calibration gaps: the gate opens at 3 calls (+0.80 logit; model 0.150 vs empirical 0.106 churn, 530 customers), under-predicts at 4 calls (0.32 vs 0.44) and is over-confident from 6 calls (0.85-0.94 vs 0.55-0.68; 39 customers). State offsets are overstated for state:46 (-1.89 vs empirical -0.91), state:5 (-1.09 vs -0.51), state:10 (-0.63 vs -0.22) and state:49 (-0.69 vs -0.32). 5667 (state:2) is a dead unit (never active). closed\_\allowbreak{}form\_\allowbreak{}max\_\allowbreak{}abs\_\allowbreak{}err 0.038 (state\_\allowbreak{}offsets, 13164 pre-activation up to 7.7) is 3-significant-figure rounding; numeric error 8.9e-16.

\subsection{Plain-language summary}\label{app:churn100-s7-c1:plain}
\noindent{\small\textit{AI-assisted draft for review (unverified). Each sentence cites the claims (C01, C02, \ldots) that back it; every cited claim was computed on the model and the training split and passed its automatic checks. Magnitudes are changes in predicted risk for a typical patient; confidence words follow the test-split check and n. The text describes what the model does, not the world.}}\par\smallskip
\paragraph{Summary (drafted).} For a typical customer (in West Virginia, area code 415, no international or voice-mail plan, 1 call to customer service and median usage) the model predicts a chance of leaving of about 1\%; it adds up five parts: usage and service calls, the international plan, fixed-weight inputs, a voice-mail and South Dakota adjustment and state adjustments.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C047]}} This part combines a usage score, built from daytime, evening and night-time minutes and the voice-mail plan, with calls to customer service, not as a simple sum.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C060]}} Customer-service calls add only from about 3 calls upwards, for most customers slowly at first, then faster, but for some customers without a voice-mail plan they add nothing until a point, then steadily: going from 0 to 4 calls takes a typical customer from about 1\% to about 15\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C055]}} Through it, daytime minutes add to the chance only above about 187 minutes for customers without a voice-mail plan, in an uneven way: for a typical customer, going from 0 to 271 minutes takes it from about 1\% to about 11\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C056]}} Daytime minutes count more with more than 201 evening minutes, in an uneven way: from about 1\% to about 11\% between 112 and 249 minutes, against about 1\% to about 2\% with fewer.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C067]}} This part reads the international plan alone and acts on the 380 of 4000 training customers who have one, 161 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 2\% without it and about 26\% with it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C078]}} For a typical customer, an international plan takes the chance of leaving from about 1\% to about 15\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C077]}} This part adds up many inputs with fixed weights, each moving a typical customer's chance by a few points at most: compared with most other states, Washington raises it to about 3\% and Montana to about 2\%, and Vermont, Rhode Island and Colorado lower it to under 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C080, C081, C082, C084, C085]}} A higher international charge raises it steadily, from under 1\% at 1.84 to about 1\% at 3.70 US dollars, and more voice-mail messages and a longer account also raise it steadily, by less than a point.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C083, C086, C098]}} More international calls lower it, each extra call taking away about the same, from about 1\% at 2 to under 1\% at 8 calls, and more evening and night-time minutes lower it steadily through this part, by less than a point.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C087, C092, C096]}} This part reads the voice-mail plan and the state: through it, a customer in South Dakota has under 1\% instead of about 1\%, and a voice-mail plan also lowers a typical customer's chance to under 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C108, C109]}} This part reads only the state: it moves a typical customer's chance from about 1\% in West Virginia to about 5\% in South Dakota and about 2\% in Indiana and in most other states, and keeps it under 1\% in Virginia (66 to 122 training customers per named state; the full list is in the technical detail).\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C111, C112, C114, C115]}}
\paragraph{The whole model.} The model adds up five parts into one score: usage and service calls, the international plan, fixed-weight inputs, a voice-mail and South Dakota adjustment, and state adjustments.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C047]}} \textit{Evidence.} It is made up of these five parts (each explained below); the score is their sum, which was checked on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C047]}} Changing one input at a time across the whole model, an international plan takes a typical customer's chance of leaving from about 1\% to about 15\%, and more daytime minutes raise it in an uneven way, from about 1\% at 112 to about 4\% at 249 minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C001, C004]}} In Washington the chance is about 5\% and in Montana about 4\%, against about 1\% in West Virginia and under 1\% in Vermont.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C002, C003, C022]}} The model ignores daytime calls, evening calls, the evening charge, international minutes and the night-time charge.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C042, C043, C044, C045, C046]}}
\paragraph{Usage and service calls.} This part raises the chance of leaving for heavy daytime users without a voice-mail plan and for customers who call customer service 3 times or more: daytime minutes in an uneven way, and calls for most customers slowly at first, then faster, but for some customers without a voice-mail plan nothing until a point, then steadily.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C056, C055]}} \textit{Evidence.} It is made up of the usage score (explained below) together with customer-service calls, combined in a way that is not a simple sum.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C060]}} Through it, daytime minutes add only above about 187 minutes for customers without a voice-mail plan, in an uneven way, from about 1\% to about 11\% between 0 and 271 minutes for a typical customer.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C056]}} Customer-service calls add only from about 3 calls upwards, for most customers slowly at first, then faster, but for some customers without a voice-mail plan nothing until a point, then steadily, from about 1\% to about 15\% between 0 and 4 calls.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C055]}}
\paragraph{Usage score.} This part builds a usage score: heavy daytime use raises the chance of leaving, in an uneven way and more so with high evening minutes, and a voice-mail plan lowers it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C071, C067, C062]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, daytime minutes add only above about 187 minutes for customers without a voice-mail plan, in an uneven way, from about 1\% to about 11\% between 0 and 271 minutes.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C071]}} Daytime minutes count more with more than 201 evening minutes (about 1\% to about 11\%, against about 1\% to about 2\%) and with more than 200 night-time minutes (about 1\% to about 7\%, against about 1\% to about 3\%), in an uneven way.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C067, C068]}} A voice-mail plan lowers the chance through it from about 3\% to about 1\% for the typical customer it acts on.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C062]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C076]}}
\paragraph{International plan.} This part raises the chance of leaving for customers with an international plan.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C077]}} \textit{Evidence.} It acts on the 380 of 4000 training customers with an international plan, 161 of whom left; for the typical customer it acts on, the chance is about 2\% without it and about 26\% with it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C078]}} For a typical customer, an international plan takes the chance from about 1\% to about 15\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C077]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C079]}}
\paragraph{Fixed-weight inputs.} This part adds small fixed-weight effects: a higher international charge, more voice-mail messages and a longer account raise the chance steadily, more international calls lower it, each extra call taking away about the same, and some states shift it up or down.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C083, C086, C098, C087, C080, C082]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, compared with most other states, Washington raises a typical customer's chance to about 3\% and Montana to about 2\%, and Vermont, Rhode Island and Colorado lower it to under 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C080, C081, C082, C084, C085]}} The international charge raises it steadily, from under 1\% at 1.84 to about 1\% at 3.70 US dollars, and international calls lower it from about 1\% at 2 to under 1\% at 8 calls, each extra call taking away about the same.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C083, C087]}} More evening and night-time minutes lower it steadily through this part, by less than a point.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C092, C096]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C107]}}
\paragraph{Voice mail and South Dakota.} This part lowers the chance of leaving for customers in South Dakota and for customers with a voice-mail plan.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C108, C109]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, a customer in South Dakota has under 1\% instead of about 1\%, and a voice-mail plan also takes a typical customer to under 1\%.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C108, C109]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C110]}}
\paragraph{State adjustments.} This part shifts the chance of leaving by state: it is lowest in West Virginia and Virginia and highest in South Dakota.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C111, C114, C115]}} \textit{Evidence.} Through it, a typical customer's chance is about 5\% in South Dakota and about 2\% in Indiana and in most other states, against about 1\% in West Virginia and under 1\% in Virginia.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C111, C112, C114, C115]}} Its formula reproduces the part exactly on all 4000 training customers.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C117]}}
\paragraph{Worth checking against what is known.} Worth checking: the state moves the chance by several points (for example Washington about 5\% and Vermont under 1\% across the whole model), based on 72 to 122 training customers per state.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C002, C022]}} Worth checking: South Dakota gets a rise through the state adjustments (to about 5\%) and a fall through the voice-mail and South Dakota adjustment (to under 1\%), so the two pull against each other.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C111, C108]}} Worth checking: more evening and night-time minutes raise the chance through the usage score but lower it through the fixed-weight inputs.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C063, C064, C092, C096]}} Worth checking: the model treats a voice-mail plan as lowering the chance of leaving but more voice-mail messages as raising it.\,{\scriptsize\textcolor{NavyBlue}{[C027, C023]}}

\paragraph{Not supported by the model.}
\begin{itemize}\setlength\itemsep{0pt}\small
\item C016: direction claim about total evening minutes in the whole model: not supported by the model (58\% of patients have the opposite sign (allowed: 10\%)).
\item C032: direction claim about total night-time minutes in the whole model: not supported by the model (63\% of patients have the opposite sign (allowed: 10\%)).
\item C058: threshold claim about total night-time minutes in part ann\_\allowbreak{}83: not supported by the model (the folds are spread over 39\% of the observed range (allowed 20\%), also within each category group: no single threshold; the effect past the fold is too small or not consistent across patients).
\item C059: threshold claim about total evening minutes in part ann\_\allowbreak{}83: not supported by the model (the effect past the fold is too small or not consistent across patients; no training patient is past the fold).
\item C069: interaction claim about total daytime minutes and voice-mail plan in part ann\_\allowbreak{}79: not supported by the model (the part's counterfactual difference has the same sign for only 89\% of affected patients).
\item C070: interaction claim about total evening minutes and voice-mail plan in part ann\_\allowbreak{}79: not supported by the model (the part's counterfactual difference has the same sign for only 89\% of affected patients).
\item C073: threshold claim about total night-time minutes in part ann\_\allowbreak{}79: not supported by the model (the folds are spread over 39\% of the observed range (allowed 20\%), also within each category group: no single threshold; the effect past the fold is too small or not consistent across patients).
\item C074: threshold claim about total evening minutes in part ann\_\allowbreak{}79: not supported by the model (the effect past the fold is too small or not consistent across patients; no training patient is past the fold).
\item C075: subgroup claim about state and voice-mail plan in part ann\_\allowbreak{}79: not supported by the model (its effect goes both ways across the patients it acts on).
\item C118: boundary claim about number of calls to customer service and total daytime minutes in part ann\_\allowbreak{}83: not supported by the model (no switch-on line could be traced on the first map to check against the data; no switch-on boundary in the observed range).
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Coverage}\label{app:churn100-s7-c1:coverage}
Coverage is computed by the current code (the function behind the \texttt{get\_coverage} tool) under these conventions. \emph{Candidate nodes} are all nodes of the explained model state except the output nodes. A candidate node is \emph{covered} when some annotation of the hierarchy (a leaf, or a composition together with its descendants) contains it and all its enabled outgoing edges. \emph{Exact Null} parts, which have no effect on any output for any input, count as covered: nodes with no path to an output over enabled, non-zero-weight edges (disconnected inputs and dead ends), and edges that have zero weight or touch such a node. Compositional coverage is the fraction of required compositions present: every annotation except a single global root containing every output must have a parent; a parentless, childless annotation made only of Null nodes is exempt.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Null, disconnected input (35):} \texttt{-11} (state:18), \texttt{-12} (state:19), \texttt{-15} (state:21), \texttt{-16} (state:22), \texttt{-17} (state:23), \texttt{-18} (state:24), \texttt{-2} (state:1), \texttt{-23} (state:29), \texttt{-24} (state:3), \texttt{-25} (state:30), \texttt{-28} (state:33), \texttt{-29} (state:34), \texttt{-31} (state:36), \texttt{-33} (state:38), \texttt{-35} (state:4), \texttt{-38} (state:42), \texttt{-39} (state:43), \texttt{-4} (state:11), \texttt{-40} (state:44), \texttt{-47} (state:50), \texttt{-48} (state:6), \texttt{-49} (state:7), \texttt{-5} (state:12), \texttt{-50} (state:8), \texttt{-51} (state:9), \texttt{-53} (areaCode:408), \texttt{-54} (areaCode:415), \texttt{-6} (state:13), \texttt{-60} (totalDayCalls), \texttt{-63} (totalEveCalls), \texttt{-64} (totalEveCharge), \texttt{-67} (totalNightCharge), \texttt{-68} (totalIntlMinutes), \texttt{-7} (state:14), \texttt{-9} (state:16).
\item \textbf{Uncovered nodes:} none.
\item \textbf{Uncovered edges:} none.
\item \textbf{Missing compositions:} none.
\end{itemize}
